text.p: A U.S. federal judge on Monday said she would approve Smith Corona Corp's plan for emerging from Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection.

In a ruling from the bench, U.S. Bankruptcy Judge Helen Balick overruled objections raised by Chase Manhattan Bank, the agent for the banks that provided Smith Corona's debtor-in-possession financing.

"I cannot permit the confirmation process to be held hostage to the banks' objection," Balick said, but she amended her order to establish her jurisdiction over any fees that the banks would charge for possible future litigation.
According to Smith Corona spokeswoman Rivian Bell, the Smith Corona plan will become effective around February 7 assuming the confirmation order is not stayed, pending an appeal by the banks.

Balick said the banks do not want their liens against Smith Corona to be discharged by a confirmation order unless they can be assured that any litigation costs that they incur will not be capped at the $650,000 proposed in the plan.
Unsecured creditors have indicated they may sue to recover pre-petition payments of up to $11 million from the banks, according to testimony in the hearing on Monday.

The company, which moved its headquarters from New Canaan, Conn., to Cortland, N.Y., has an agreement with Congress Financial Corp for a $25 million credit facility to support the operations of the reorganized business.
Under the plan, unsecured creditors will receive about $0.36 in cash for each dollar of allowed claims.

They will also receive 85 percent of common stock in the new company to be issued on the effective date of the plan. The company has applied to be listed on the Nasdaq, and the number of shares to be issued is not to exceed 3.3 million shares, according to court papers.

Current shareholders will receive one warrant for every 20 shares of Smith Corona stock they now hold. The warrants will be priced at $8.50 each and can be exercised during a period that begins six months after the effective date and ends 18 months later.
KPMG Peat Marwick LLP senior manager Daniel Polsky testified to a valuation range for Smith Corona of $14.9 million to $21.1 million with a midpoint value of $18 million.

Polsky told Reuters: "I think the company has some interesting prospective product offerings in the consumer electronics and telephony areas which should spark both retailer and consumser interest and will restore Smith Corona to its former level of promise."
Smith Corona makes personal word processors and portable electric typewriters. The company filed for Chapter 11 protection on July 5, 1995.
